blocks.text: At the baptism of Christ there are some of the Fathers who hold that a real dove descended. [col. 35] Thus Tertullian, in the book On the Flesh of Christ, chapter 3, writes of the Spirit descending upon Christ: It was as truly a dove as it was also spirit; nor had it destroyed ^{a)} its own substance by assuming a foreign substance. And Augustine, On the Christian Combat, ch. 22, comparing the body of Christ with this dove, says: Nor do we say this in such a way as to say that the Lord Jesus alone had a true body, while the Holy Spirit appeared deceptively to the eyes of men; rather, we believe both those bodies to be true bodies. For just as it was not fitting that the Son of God should deceive men, so it was not becoming that the Holy Spirit should deceive men. But for almighty God, who made the whole creation out of nothing, it was not difficult to form a true body of a dove without the agency of other doves, just as it was not difficult for him to make a true body in the womb of Mary without male seed. Yet the four Evangelists ^{b)} do not say that a dove descended upon Christ, but ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν [hōsei peristeran], as a dove. And Luke more explicitly says that the Holy Spirit descended σωματικῷ εἴδει ὡσεὶ περιστερὰν [sōmatikō eidei hōsei peristeran], in bodily form as a dove. There the Syriac has ܒܕܡܘܬܐ ܓܘܫܡܐ ܕܝܘܢܐ, after the likeness of the body of a dove. And the Arabic, شبه جسد حمامة [shibh jasad ḥamāma] in the likeness of the body of a dove. And the Ethiopic, በሥጋ፡ ከመ፡ ርእየተ፡ ርግብ፡ In a body as in the appearance of a dove. From this one may conclude that, in the Ethiopic translator's mind, what appeared was a body, but not the body of a real dove. St Augustine is followed by Thomas in the Summa, part 3, question 39, article 7. Indeed Sixtus of Siena, Biblioth. book 6, annotation 13, writes that almost all the Scholastic theologians hold the same view. Most of the more recent writers, however, think otherwise, namely that the Spirit descended not in a real dove but in the appearance of a dove. Caring little about Tertullian, they evade Augustine's authority in two ways. Some, like Pamelius, deny that the book On the Christian Combat is really Augustine's. Others, like Maldonatus, accept it as genuine, but contend that Augustine asserts only that a true body appeared, not however a real dove. But neither party is convincing.

[II, 569] Not the first, since it is established that the book On the Combat is Augustine's, both from its style and from Possidius' Indiculus and from Augustine himself, who acknowledges that book as his own in book 2 of the Retractations, ch. 3. Not the second, because Augustine calls that dove not only a true body but also a true body of a dove. It was not difficult for God, he says, to form a true body of a dove without the agency of other doves. In his opinion this was necessary so that the Holy Spirit should not deceive men, if that dove [col. 36] had not been what it seemed to be. He holds, therefore, that this dove was as truly a dove as Christ was truly a man. Accordingly I would say of both, that is, of Augustine as well as of Tertullian, that in arguing against those who held that Christ's body was as imaginary as that dove was, they erred, as often happens, τῇ τῆς ἀνθόλκης ἀμετρίᾳ [tē tēs anthol kēs ametria]. For although it would have sufficed to assert the reality of Christ's body, they wanted even this φάσμα ὄρνιθος [phasma ornithos], as Origen rightly calls it, to be taken for a real dove. But four things are to be noted here. First, outside the heat of controversy the same writers define it otherwise. For in Tertullian, book On Baptism, ch. 8, we read that the Holy Spirit descended upon the Lord in the figure of a dove. And in Augustine's Letter 102 to Evodius this dove is said to have been presented to the eyes in bodily appearance only, not expressed in the nature of a living animal. And in On the Trinity, book 2, ch. 5: Upon the Lord himself (the Holy Spirit) descended in bodily form, like a dove. Second, other Fathers regarded this dove as imaginary. Justin, in the Dialogue with Trypho the Jew: Τοῦ ἐπελθόντος ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς πνεύματος [tou epelthontos en eidei peristeras pneumatos]. Irenaeus, book 3, ch. 19: They said that the Spirit of God descended upon him like a dove. Origen on Luke, Homily 27: The Holy Spirit descended upon the Saviour in the appearance of a dove. Epiphanius against the Sabellians, Heresy 62: Ἐν εἴδει περιστερᾶς σχηματίζεται [en eidei peristeras schēmatizetai]. And the translator: He conformed himself to the likeness of a dove. Hilary on Matthew, Canon 2: The Holy Spirit is sent forth, and is recognized as visible in the appearance of a dove. Nonnus in the Paraphrase of St John calls it Ἀντίτυπον μίμημα πελειάδος [antitypon mimēma peleiados]. Juvencus, Evang. Hist. book 1:
And bearing bodily form, the Spirit descended from on high, imitating from the cloud an airy dove.
At once the heavens opened, and the Holy Spirit in the appearance of a dove clothed Christ with honour.
